prompt: Which set of side lengths could NOT form a triangle?
hint: Three lengths form a triangle only if the two shorter sides can reach past the ends of the longest side. Test that idea on each set.

hints.text: Three lengths form a triangle only if the two shorter sides can reach past the ends of the longest side. Test that idea on each set.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try an obvious failure: $1$, $2$, and $9$ cannot close, since $1 + 2 = 3 < 9$. Compare the two shortest sides against the longest — that one check is enough.
In each choice, add the two shorter lengths and compare the sum with the longest. For choice B, compare $3 + 4$ with $8$.
Since $3 + 4 = 7$ is less than $8$, the lengths $3$, $4$, $8$ cannot form a triangle, which is choice B.

explanation: The Triangle Inequality says the sum of any two sides must be greater than the third side. Checking the two shortest against the longest is enough.
Choice A works because $5 + 7 = 12 > 10$, choice C works because $6 + 6 = 12 > 6$, and choice D works because $8 + 15 = 23 > 17$.
Choice B fails, because $3 + 4 = 7$ is less than $8$ and the two short sides cannot meet.
The set that could not form a triangle is $3$, $4$, $8$, which is choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Picture the two short sides swinging shut
steps: Imagine the two shorter sides as hinged arms attached to the ends of the longest side.
If they are too short to meet in the middle, no triangle exists — they cannot reach across.
Checking the two shortest against the longest is sufficient; the other two comparisons are then automatic.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Testing the wrong pair — say 4 + 8 against 3 — passes everything and finds no failure.
The only test that matters: the two SHORTEST sides against the longest. If that pair fails, the triangle is impossible; if it passes, all pairs pass.
